senses.gloss: So correct that nobody can find fault with it.
examples: Her conduct during the investigation was *irreproachable*.
He has an *irreproachable* record after thirty years on the job.
The hotel's service is *irreproachable*.

contrast: Spelled *-ible*, not *-able*.

senses.gloss: So attractive or tempting that you cannot say no.
examples: The dessert menu was *irresistible*.
She has an almost *irresistible* smile.
The offer was *irresistible* to a kid who had never flown before.

senses.gloss: Too strong to be stopped or held back.
examples: He felt an *irresistible* urge to laugh.
By spring the case for reform had become *irresistible*.

senses.gloss: Not thinking about the harm your actions may do.
examples: It was *irresponsible* to leave the kids alone.
He is a nice guy, but completely *irresponsible* with money.
Printing a rumor like that is *irresponsible* journalism.

senses.gloss: Impossible to get back or to put right again.
examples: The fire did *irretrievable* damage to the archive.
Deleted files are not always *irretrievable*.
The court found an *irretrievable* breakdown of the marriage.

senses.gloss: Making fun of things other people treat as serious or sacred.
examples: The show takes an *irreverent* look at Washington.
His humor is *irreverent* but never cruel.
Some readers found the cartoon *irreverent*.

senses.gloss: Impossible to change back to how it was.
examples: The damage to her hearing is *irreversible*.
Scientists warn of *irreversible* changes to the coastline.
Once you sign, the decision is *irreversible*.

contrast: The stress falls on the second syllable — *i-REV-uh-kuh-buhl*, not on *-voke*.

senses.gloss: Final, so that it cannot be canceled or taken back.
examples: The offer is *irrevocable* for thirty days.
She made an *irrevocable* decision to leave the company.
The bank issued an *irrevocable* letter of credit.

contrast: *Irritable* is the person's mood; *irritating* is the thing that causes it.

senses.gloss: Easily annoyed, usually because of tiredness or stress.
examples: He gets *irritable* when he is hungry.
After three hours of sleep she was *irritable* all morning.
Do not take it personally — he is just in an *irritable* mood.

senses.gloss: Belonging to Islam or to the countries where it is the main religion.
examples: *Islamic* art fills two rooms of the museum.
She teaches a course on *Islamic* law.
The mosque is a landmark of *Islamic* architecture.

senses.gloss: Far from other places or other people.
examples: They live on an *isolated* farm in Montana.
After the move she felt *isolated* and homesick.

senses.gloss: Happening only once, not part of a pattern.
examples: The police called it an *isolated* incident.
There were *isolated* reports of flooding in the valley.

contrast: Also a noun for the person: *the isolationists in Congress*.

senses.gloss: Wanting a country to stay out of other countries' affairs.
examples: He ran on an *isolationist* foreign policy.
*Isolationist* sentiment grew through the 1930s.
The party took an *isolationist* turn after the war.

senses.gloss: Of exercise, working the muscle without moving the joint.
examples: The physical therapist gave her *isometric* exercises.
*Isometric* training builds strength without movement.

senses.gloss: Of a drawing, showing three sides at equal angles.
examples: The plans use an *isometric* projection.
He drew the room in *isometric* view.

senses.gloss: Of a triangle, having two sides of equal length.
examples: An *isosceles* triangle has two equal sides.
Draw an *isosceles* triangle with a four-inch base.
The roof forms a nearly perfect *isosceles* triangle.

contrast: The noun is normally plural: *set the title in italics*.

senses.gloss: Of type, sloping to the right.
examples: Book titles go in *italic* type.
Use an *italic* font for the quotations.
The *italic* letters are hard to read at that size.

senses.gloss: Feeling an unpleasant tickle on the skin, or causing one.
examples: My eyes get *itchy* every spring.
That wool sweater is *itchy*.
The rash is *itchier* at night than during the day.

senses.gloss: Done by repeating a cycle and improving it each time.
examples: The team uses an *iterative* design process.
The algorithm takes an *iterative* approach to the answer.
Writing is *iterative* — you draft, you cut, you draft again.

senses.gloss: Traveling from place to place to work.
examples: He was an *itinerant* preacher in the 1930s.
*Itinerant* workers followed the harvest north.
She spent ten years as an *itinerant* musician.

contrast: Baby talk or a joke; the neutral word is *tiny*.

senses.gloss: Very small.
examples: There is an *itsy-bitsy* spider in the tub.
She wore an *itsy-bitsy* yellow polka-dot bikini.
He left me an *itsy-bitsy* piece of cake.

senses.gloss: Very small.
examples: They live in an *itty-bitty* apartment downtown.
The puppy was an *itty-bitty* thing when we got him.
I only had an *itty-bitty* taste of it.

senses.gloss: Bored and no longer excited, after too much of something.
examples: After twenty years in the business he is pretty *jaded*.
*Jaded* voters stayed home on election day.
She was *jaded* about dating apps long before she quit them.

contrast: The *-ed* is a full syllable — *JAG-id*, not *jagd*.

senses.gloss: Having a rough, uneven edge with sharp points.
examples: He cut his foot on a *jagged* piece of glass.
The coastline here is rocky and *jagged*.
A *jagged* line ran down the middle of the screen.

senses.gloss: Completely full of people or things.
examples: The stadium was *jam-packed* an hour before kickoff.
The book is *jam-packed* with photographs.
We rode a *jam-packed* subway car to the game.

contrast: Also a noun for the person: *she's a Jamaican*.

senses.gloss: From Jamaica, or belonging to it.
examples: *Jamaican* coffee is expensive for a reason.
The restaurant serves *Jamaican* food.
Her mother is *Jamaican*.

senses.gloss: Stuck so that it will not move or work.
examples: The copier is *jammed* again.
He could not get the *jammed* window open.

senses.gloss: Filled with too many people or things.
examples: The highway was *jammed* with traffic.
We squeezed into a *jammed* elevator.

form: -ing from *jar* — to give an unpleasant shock

senses.gloss: Unpleasantly surprising because it does not fit.
examples: The ending was *jarring*.
There is a *jarring* shift in tone halfway through the book.
It is *jarring* to hear your own voice recorded.

position: both — the figurative sense almost always before a noun

senses.gloss: Seeing things bitterly and suspiciously after bad experience.
examples: He takes a *jaundiced* view of campaign promises.
She looked at the new plan with a *jaundiced* eye.

senses.gloss: Having yellow skin and eyes because of liver trouble.
examples: The newborn was slightly *jaundiced* for a few days.
His skin looked *jaundiced* under the lamp.

senses.gloss: Cheerful and confident in a lively, stylish way.
examples: He wore his hat at a *jaunty* angle.
She came in with a *jaunty* step.
His mood was *jauntier* than it had been all week.

senses.gloss: Sounding like jazz.
examples: The soundtrack has a *jazzy* feel.
They played a *jazzy* version of the old hymn.

senses.gloss: Bright and showy.
examples: He showed up in a *jazzy* orange tie.
The new logo is a lot *jazzier* than the old one.

senses.gloss: Belonging to Thomas Jefferson's ideas of limited government and independent citizens.
examples: He appealed to *Jeffersonian* ideals of small government.
*Jeffersonian* democracy rested on the independent farmer.
The essay traces the *Jeffersonian* strain in American politics.

contrast: Also a noun, the dried meat: *beef jerky*.

senses.gloss: Moving in sudden, uneven starts and stops.
examples: The camera work is *jerky* and hard to watch.
The old elevator starts with a *jerky* motion.
His movements got *jerkier* as he tired.

senses.gloss: Deep, shiny black.
examples: She has *jet-black* hair.
The horse was *jet-black* except for one white foot.
He drives a *jet-black* pickup.

contrast: American spelling has one *l*; British writing has *jewelled*.

senses.gloss: Decorated with jewels.
examples: She wore a *jeweled* bracelet.
The crown has a *jeweled* cross on top.
A *jeweled* dagger sat in the display case.

contrast: Also a noun for the person, and also written *jihadist*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to armed Islamist groups that call their fight a holy war.
examples: The group ran a network of *jihadi* websites.
He was tried on charges of *jihadi* recruitment.
*Jihadi* propaganda spread through the app.

senses.gloss: Suddenly left by a lover or a fiancé.
examples: The story is told by a *jilted* bride.
A *jilted* boyfriend keyed her car.
He plays the *jilted* lover in the second act.

senses.gloss: Loudly patriotic in an aggressive way toward other countries.
examples: The coverage turned *jingoistic* once the war started.
He gave a *jingoistic* speech about national greatness.
Critics called the movie *jingoistic*.

senses.gloss: Seeming to bring bad luck, or to have it.
examples: That car is *jinxed* — it has broken down four times.
I felt *jinxed* after losing three games in a row.
The whole project seemed *jinxed* from the start.

senses.gloss: Nervous and unable to keep still.
examples: Three cups of coffee made me *jittery*.
Investors are *jittery* about the election.
She gets *jittery* before a presentation.

contrast: *Jobless* is the newspaper word and also describes figures (*jobless claims*); *unemployed* is the more formal one for a person.

senses.gloss: Without paid work.
examples: He has been *jobless* since the plant closed.
*Jobless* claims fell again last month.
Thousands of workers were left *jobless*.

contrast: Also a common noun: *a knee joint*, and informally a place — *a pizza joint*.

senses.gloss: Done, owned or shared by two or more people or groups.
examples: They filed a *joint* tax return.
The two countries issued a *joint* statement.
It was a *joint* effort by three departments.

contrast: Also a noun for the person: *two Jordanians were on the flight*.

senses.gloss: From Jordan, or belonging to it.
examples: The *Jordanian* government denied the report.
We met a *Jordanian* student at the conference.
Her husband is *Jordanian*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the work of reporters and news writing.
examples: The piece fails basic *journalistic* standards.
She won the prize for *journalistic* integrity.
*Journalistic* sources are protected by law in most states.

senses.gloss: Cheerful and friendly, often loudly so.
examples: Our host was loud and *jovial*.
He was in a *jovial* mood all evening.
A *jovial* man in a red sweater handed out cider.

senses.gloss: Full of happiness, or showing it.
examples: It was a *joyful* reunion.
The choir sang a *joyful* hymn.
Everyone looked *joyful* when the news came through.

senses.gloss: Giving or showing no pleasure at all.
examples: It was a *joyless* meal in a silent kitchen.
The work became *joyless* after the reorganization.
She described her childhood as *joyless*.

contrast: Formal or literary; in ordinary speech Americans say *joyful* or just *happy*.

senses.gloss: Full of great happiness.
examples: It was a *joyous* occasion for the whole family.
The crowd let out a *joyous* shout.
The entire weekend was *joyous*.

senses.gloss: Openly delighted, usually after a win or good news.
examples: *Jubilant* fans poured onto the field.
She was *jubilant* after the verdict.
A *jubilant* crowd filled the square until midnight.

senses.gloss: Shared by the Jewish and Christian traditions.
examples: He appealed to *Judeo-Christian* values.
The course covers the *Judeo-Christian* tradition.
*Judeo-Christian* ethics shaped the law of that period.

contrast: American spelling drops the *e*: *judgmental*, *judgment*.

senses.gloss: Too quick to criticize other people.
examples: I do not want to sound *judgmental*, but that was a mistake.
She is *judgmental* about how other people raise their kids.
He gave me a *judgmental* look over his glasses.

contrast: *Judicial* means "of the courts"; *judicious* means "showing good judgment".

senses.gloss: Having to do with courts, judges and the law.
examples: The law faces *judicial* review in the fall.
*Judicial* appointments to that court are for life.
She built her career in the *judicial* branch.

contrast: Not the same word as *judicial*, which is about courts.

senses.gloss: Showing good sense and careful judgment.
examples: A *judicious* use of salt makes all the difference.
He was *judicious* about what he said in public.
The editor made a few *judicious* cuts.

senses.gloss: Full of juice.
examples: These peaches are *juicy*.
This one is *juicier* than the last.

senses.gloss: Interesting because it is scandalous or full of gossip.
examples: She has all the *juicy* details.
The book is full of *juicy* stories about the studio.

senses.gloss: Mixed together with no order.
examples: The papers were *jumbled* in a cardboard box.
Her notes are a *jumbled* mess.
My memory of that night is *jumbled*.

senses.gloss: Much bigger than the usual size, especially of a product.
examples: She ordered a *jumbo* box of popcorn.
*Jumbo* shrimp cost more per pound.
The store sells eggs in a *jumbo* size.

senses.gloss: Nervous and easily startled.
examples: The dog is *jumpy* around strangers.
I have been *jumpy* ever since the break-in.
He gets *jumpier* the closer we get to the deadline.

contrast: Also a noun: *a junior in high school*, *she's the junior on the team*.

senses.gloss: Lower in rank, or younger.
examples: She is a *junior* partner at the firm.
Two *junior* staffers wrote the report.
He is *junior* to me by three years.

form: compound — noun + participle, from sailing, where a *jury mast* was a temporary one
contrast: Often mixed up with *jerry-built*, which means badly built rather than temporary.

senses.gloss: Put together quickly from whatever was on hand.
examples: They sailed home under a *jury-rigged* mast.
The whole setup is *jury-rigged* with duct tape.
He built a *jury-rigged* antenna out of a coat hanger.

contrast: The adjective means "fair". The everyday *just* in *I just got here* is an adverb and a different use altogether.

senses.gloss: Fair and morally right.
examples: It was a *just* decision.
They spent their lives fighting for a *just* society.
The punishment seemed *just* to everyone in the room.

senses.gloss: Able to be defended as reasonable or right.
examples: The expense is *justifiable* given the results.
The court ruled it was *justifiable* self-defense.
Her anger was entirely *justifiable*.

senses.gloss: Having a good reason; fair in the circumstances.
examples: Her complaint was fully *justified*.
You were *justified* in walking out of that meeting.

senses.gloss: Of text, spaced so that both margins line up evenly.
examples: The columns are *justified* on both sides.
Set the paragraph to *justified* rather than ragged right.

contrast: Also a noun in legal and news writing: *a juvenile was arrested*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with young people below the legal adult age.
examples: The case went to *juvenile* court.
*Juvenile* crime dropped sharply in the 1990s.

senses.gloss: Childish in a way that annoys adults.
examples: His jokes are *juvenile*.
Stop being so *juvenile* about it.

senses.gloss: Placed side by side so that the difference shows.
examples: The two photographs are *juxtaposed* on facing pages.
The *juxtaposed* images make the point better than any caption.
Her calm voice, *juxtaposed* with the sirens, was eerie.

senses.gloss: Nightmarishly confusing and impersonal, like the bureaucracy in Kafka's novels.
examples: Getting the permit was a *Kafkaesque* ordeal.
The whole appeals process felt *Kafkaesque*.
He describes a *Kafkaesque* maze of forms and phone trees.

senses.gloss: Made of many bright parts that keep shifting.
examples: The film offers a *kaleidoscopic* view of the city.
Sunlight through the glass made a *kaleidoscopic* pattern on the floor.
Her novels are *kaleidoscopic* — dozens of voices at once.

position: predicative only — after a verb: *the TV is kaput*, never *a kaput TV*
contrast: Informal and a little jokey; in writing use *broken* or *out of order*.

senses.gloss: Broken and finished, beyond repair.
examples: The washing machine is *kaput*.
My old laptop finally went *kaput*.
After the storm the generator was *kaput*.

contrast: Also a noun for the person and for the language.

senses.gloss: From Kashmir, or belonging to it.
examples: She bought a *Kashmiri* shawl.
*Kashmiri* cooking uses a lot of saffron.
His grandparents were *Kashmiri*.

contrast: Also a noun for the person: *three Kenyans finished in the top ten*.

senses.gloss: From Kenya, or belonging to it.
examples: The *Kenyan* runners swept the race.
We had *Kenyan* coffee at breakfast.
Her father is *Kenyan*.

contrast: Also a very common noun: *house keys*, *the key to the puzzle*.

senses.gloss: Most important; the one the rest depends on.
examples: She played a *key* role in the negotiations.
*Key* witnesses refused to testify.
Timing is *key* to the whole plan.

senses.gloss: Working without a physical key.
examples: The car has *keyless* entry.
Our front door uses a *keyless* lock.
*Keyless* ignition became standard on that model.

contrast: Said KAYN-, not KEEN-, because the name *Keynes* rhymes with *rains*.

senses.gloss: Following Keynes's idea that government spending should support demand.
examples: The stimulus was a classic *Keynesian* response.
He teaches *Keynesian* economics.
*Keynesian* policy favors spending in a downturn.

contrast: Also a noun; the plural *khakis* means the pants themselves.

senses.gloss: Of a dull yellowish-brown color.
examples: He wore a *khaki* jacket.
The uniform was *khaki* with brown boots.
She bought two pairs of *khaki* pants.

senses.gloss: Naturally kind and generous toward others.
examples: She is the most *kindhearted* person I know.
He was a gruff but *kindhearted* old man.
A *kindhearted* neighbor shoveled our walk.

contrast: *Kindly* is far more common as an adverb (*kindly step back*); as an adjective it is slightly old-fashioned and usually sits before a noun.

senses.gloss: Kind and gentle in manner.
examples: A *kindly* woman showed us the way to the station.
He had a *kindly* face and a slow way of talking.
She was *kindlier* to strangers than to her own family.

contrast: Nearly always in the fixed phrase *a kindred spirit*, meaning someone who thinks and feels as you do.

senses.gloss: Of the same kind, or feeling the same way.
examples: We were *kindred* spirits from the first conversation.
The two languages are *kindred* tongues.
They share a *kindred* interest in old maps.

senses.gloss: Having to do with movement, especially in physics.
examples: *Kinetic* energy depends on mass and speed.
The museum has a room of *kinetic* sculpture.

senses.gloss: Full of fast, restless energy.
examples: The dance number is wildly *kinetic*.
His prose has a *kinetic* rhythm to it.

contrast: Also written *king-sized*; both are normal in American English.

senses.gloss: Of the largest size made, especially of a bed.
examples: We slept in a *king-size* bed.
He bought a *king-size* candy bar.
The room comes with a *king-size* mattress.

contrast: The sexual meaning is the one most listeners hear first, so *kinky hair* can sound like a joke; many Americans say *coily* or *tightly curled* instead.

senses.gloss: Involving unusual sexual tastes.
examples: The novel has a *kinky* streak running through it.
He had some *kinky* ideas about the costume party.

senses.gloss: Of hair, wire or cord, full of tight curls or bends.
examples: Her hair is thick and *kinky*.
The cord got *kinkier* every time we coiled it.

senses.gloss: Cheap and tasteless, often in a way people enjoy on purpose.
examples: The lobby is full of *kitschy* souvenirs.
I love how *kitschy* that diner is.
Their decorations get *kitschier* every Christmas.

senses.gloss: Deep enough to reach the knees.
examples: We waded through *knee-deep* water.
The snow was *knee-deep* by morning.

senses.gloss: Deeply involved in something, usually work or trouble.
examples: He is *knee-deep* in paperwork.
By then she was *knee-deep* in the investigation.

senses.gloss: Long enough to reach the knee.
examples: She wore a *knee-length* skirt.
*Knee-length* boots are back in style.
The coat is *knee-length*.

contrast: *Knit* works as the adjective too, and is more common in short phrases: *a knit cap*.

senses.gloss: Made by knitting yarn.
examples: She gave me a *knitted* scarf.
He pulled on a *knitted* hat.
The store sells *knitted* blankets.

senses.gloss: Covered with small round lumps.
examples: The old tree has *knobby* roots.
He had *knobby* knees and long arms.
These tires are *knobbier* than the ones made for pavement.

senses.gloss: Able to be known or found out.
examples: Some things are simply not *knowable*.
The exact number is not *knowable* from the records we have.
He wanted a *knowable* answer, not a guess.

contrast: A *knowing* look means the person is in on a secret; it does not mean "well informed" — that is *knowledgeable*.

senses.gloss: Showing that you understand something others have not said out loud.
examples: She gave me a *knowing* smile.
There was a *knowing* look between the two of them.
He answered with a *knowing* nod.

senses.gloss: Knowing a lot about something.
examples: The salesperson was very *knowledgeable* about bikes.
We need a *knowledgeable* guide for the canyon.
She is the most *knowledgeable* person on the team.

contrast: Before a noun it means "recognized, on record": *a known problem*. After a verb, *known as* and *known for* are the passive verb, not this adjective.

senses.gloss: Recognized or established as a fact.
examples: He is a *known* troublemaker in the building.
The side effects are a *known* risk.
There is no *known* cure.

senses.gloss: Strange in a harmless, funny way.
examples: She has a *kooky* sense of humor.
The neighbors are friendly but a little *kooky*.
His theories get *kookier* every year.

senses.gloss: Prepared according to Jewish dietary law.
examples: The deli is strictly *kosher*.
We bought *kosher* salt for the recipe.

senses.gloss: Honest and above board.
examples: Something about the deal did not seem *kosher*.
Is it *kosher* to email him directly?

contrast: Also the name of the language: *he speaks Kurdish*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the Kurds or their region.
examples: *Kurdish* forces held the north of the country.
He comes from a *Kurdish* family.
The village is mostly *Kurdish*.

contrast: Also a noun for the person: *two Kuwaitis signed the deal*.

senses.gloss: From Kuwait, or belonging to it.
examples: The *Kuwaiti* government funded the hospital.
He works for a *Kuwaiti* oil company.
Her business partner is *Kuwaiti*.

contrast: American spelling has one *l*; British writing has *labelled*.

senses.gloss: Marked with a label saying what it is.
examples: Every box was clearly *labeled*.
Keep the leftovers in a *labeled* container.
The wires were not *labeled*, so we had to guess.

contrast: American spelling *labor*; British writing has *labour-intensive*.

senses.gloss: Needing a lot of人 work by hand.
examples: Picking the fruit by hand is *labor-intensive*.
It is a *labor-intensive* process that cannot be automated.
The new method is less *labor-intensive* than the old one.

contrast: American spelling *labored*; British writing has *laboured*.

senses.gloss: Slow and difficult, especially of breathing or movement.
examples: His breathing was *labored*.
She climbed the last flight with *labored* steps.

senses.gloss: Sounding forced instead of natural.
examples: The joke felt *labored*.
The essay ends on a *labored* note.

senses.gloss: Taking a lot of time and hard, dull effort.
examples: Copying the records by hand was *laborious*.
It is a *laborious* process, but it works.
He described the *laborious* business of restoring the piano.

senses.gloss: Having no end or no boundary.
examples: The job offers almost *limitless* opportunities.
Her patience seemed *limitless*.
Storage space is cheap, but it is not *limitless*.

contrast: Also a verb and a noun: *he walks with a limp*.

senses.gloss: Soft and drooping, with no stiffness or strength.
examples: The lettuce had gone *limp* in the fridge.
He gave me a *limp* handshake.
The flowers looked *limper* every day.

senses.gloss: Going straight from start to finish, in order.
examples: The movie does not tell the story in a *linear* way.
We expected *linear* progress and got none.

senses.gloss: In math, involving a straight-line relationship.
examples: The two variables have a *linear* relationship.
Solve the *linear* equation for x.

senses.gloss: Having a layer of material on the inside.
examples: She wore a *lined* raincoat.
The jewelry box is *lined* with velvet.

senses.gloss: Printed with straight lines to write on.
examples: He writes his drafts on *lined* paper.
Bring a *lined* notebook to class.

senses.gloss: Marked with wrinkles.
examples: His face was deeply *lined*.
She had the *lined* hands of a gardener.

senses.gloss: Having to do with language or the study of it.
examples: *Linguistic* differences made the negotiation harder.
She studies the *linguistic* history of the region.
The test measures *linguistic* ability.

senses.gloss: Joined or connected to something else.
examples: The two accounts are *linked*.
Smoking is *linked* to heart disease.
*Linked* devices share the same settings.

contrast: Also a common noun: *pour the liquid into a bowl*.

senses.gloss: In the form of a liquid, not solid and not gas.
examples: The medicine comes in *liquid* form.
Add the *liquid* ingredients last.

senses.gloss: Of money or property, easy to turn into cash.
examples: Most of their money is not *liquid*.
The fund keeps some *liquid* assets on hand.
